Apache Arrow · WebAssembly components · Rust · Go · Python · TypeScript · Kotlin · C#

Batch pipelines that
work out their own order

SACI is a columnar batch processing engine for Rust, built on Apache Arrow. You write transforms in Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, or C# and say which columns each one reads and writes. SACI derives the execution plan, runs independent work concurrently, and loads the whole pipeline as a WebAssembly component.

Run the service Use it as a library
License AGPL-3.0-only Rust 1.95+ Status experimental

Two ways to use SACI

The pipeline code is the same either way. The choice is who owns the process: one binary you configure, or your own binary that links the engine.

Service

Run the service

A KDL file names the sources, formats, processors and sinks. One binary runs it, and a processor is a WebAssembly component in Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin or C#.

 As a Library

Embed the engine

saci-core in your own crate. You own main and call pipeline.run(), with a debugger on the same process.

Is SACI a fit?

Reach for SACI when
  • Work arrives as batches of 100k to 100M rows, or as a stream of individual items
  • The transform is imperative code that SQL expresses awkwardly
  • Schemas are wide: tens to hundreds of columns, and each step reads a few
  • You need recovery time to be a design constraint, not an afterthought
Look elsewhere when
  • You want SQL. There is no query planner here; DataFusion will win
  • You need hard real-time guarantees. Stream mode is sub-millisecond per item in-process, but it is not a real-time scheduler
  • You need exactly-once delivery. Recovery is at-least-once, so a sink has to tolerate the same batch twice
  • Your data is under ~10k rows. A plain Vec will beat this

Why columns

Storing each field as a contiguous Arrow column, instead of a row per record, changes what the machine has to move.

▮

Read only what you touch

A system reading 3 of 50 columns loads 24 MB instead of 400 MB per million rows. The rest never enters cache.

⇄

Handoff is a pointer

Passing a batch between stages is an Arc clone: one atomic increment, no buffer copy.

◇

Checkpoints are a memcpy

Arrow IPC writes contiguous buffers, so crash recovery decodes 6× faster than a row-oriented equivalent at 1M rows.

See the benchmark numbers and how they were measured

Where the name comes from

SACI is Self-orchestrated Autonomous Compute Interface. Self-orchestrated because you never write a stage list: each System declares the Arrow fields it reads and writes, and the schedule follows from those declarations alone. The Component and System vocabulary comes from ECS, the Entity Component System pattern from game development, which organises game entities as components that systems act on each frame. SACI swaps the entity for a data Pipeline. A frame of entities becomes a batch of Arrow columns, and systems group by the fields each one names rather than by whole components.

Prior art

Conduit is the strongest influence on this project. It streams data between stores in Go, and builds a pipeline from source and destination connectors plus processors. The plugin contract is language-agnostic, so a connector can be written in anything. Standalone processors run as WebAssembly, and Conduit either embeds in your own binary or runs as a service you hand a config to. Every one of those Conduit shapes is here, with a WIT world in place of the gRPC interface.

The unit of work differs. A Conduit pipeline carries records; a SACI pipeline carries Arrow batches, and works out its execution order from the columns each system declares.

Where this project is

SACI explores two questions: how far specialised coding agents can maintain a non-trivial multi-crate Rust codebase, and what a Rust-native batch engine with WebAssembly extensibility should look like. It is not production-ready, and the crates are not published to crates.io. Feedback and contributions are welcome.
